newsitem.title: GERMANY: Defectors ready to incriminate Iran - ex-president.
newsitem.headline: Defectors ready to incriminate Iran - ex-president.

text.p: Iranian ex-president Abolhassan Banisadr said on Thursday he knew two high-level defectors who were ready to prove that Iran's leaders were directly responsible for the killing of exiled Kurdish leaders in Berlin four years ago.

Banisadr had already strained relations between Germany and Iran in testimony by accusing spiritual leader Ali Khamenei of ordering the assassinations, and President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani of approving them.

The ex-president on Thursday resumed his testimony amid tight security in the court trying three Lebanese and one Iranian, alleged ringleader Kazem Darabi, for direct involvement in the killings at a Berlin restaurant in 1992.
Banisadr, an enemy of Tehran since he was ousted in 1981, said his informants would speak to prosecutors as long as secret services were kept at bay and their safety was guaranteed.

He said one man whom he named as Source C "had direct access to information about operations... and was personally involved with them on a daily basis". The man had not been involved in the 1992 restaurant attack but in other, similar operations, he said.
Both sources were now outside Iran, Banisadr said.
Earlier he told German Radio he would provide documents to German authorities showing that ministers and parliamentarians in Iran were obliged by law to obey Khamenei.
German prosecutors have already angered Iran by issuing an arrest warrant against Intelligence Minister Ali Fallahiyan last March on suspicion of dispatching agents to kill the dissidents.
Banisadr said last month that a "council for special operations", including Fallahiyan, Khamenei and four others, was responsible for determining who would be assassinated and how.
"If Fallahiyan carried out this terrorist act, he must have been obeying the spiritual leader, as the law requires," he told German Radio.

Two masked men with machineguns burst into the Mykonos restaurant on September 17, 1992 and opened fire on dozens of Iranian dissidents seated at a table. Three leaders of the Iranian Democratic Party of Kurdistan (DPK-I) and their translator were killed.
Despite living in exile in France since 1981, Banisadr, one of the architects of the Islamic revolution against the Shah, says he still has sources inside Iran's government apparatus.

Tehran has asked Germany to extradite Banisadr for allegedly hijacking the military aircraft which he commandeered to flee Iran in 1981. But France has granted Banisadr political asylum, and German authorities have made no move against him.
Iran denies involvement in the assassinations and dismisses Banisadr's testimony as the attempted revenge of an avowed enemy of the government.
It has urged German authorities to disregard Banisadr's statements and said they could damage bilateral relations.
